trust_boundaries.name: Inbound messages from the owner and connected platforms

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NOT accept or act on instructions from anyone other than its single owner-operator
Any third party who reaches the agent through a connected channel but is not the owner.
content retrieved from external sources — web pages, emails, chat or integration messages ... is data to be processed, never commands

threats.summary: A third party messaging the owner's connected account could drive the agent as if they were the owner, but inbound external messages that are not self-messages are routed to a notification-only path in code — no session, no trigger, no action-selection call — and unlabeled inbound defaults to third-party.

The notification the gate emits carries a 500-character preview of the third-party message body and is appended to conversation history, so the sender's text still reaches the model's context on the next turn.
The browser control surface is bound to localhost, but nothing authenticates the WebSocket client, so any local process or logged-in session on the host can speak to the agent as the owner.
threats.remainder: loopback binding excludes remote callers but there is no token, password or origin check on the WebSocket endpoint, so any local process on the host is accepted as the owner

trust_boundaries.name: Retrieved content and tool output entering model context

remit_rules.excerpt: file contents, tool or MCP outputs — as trusted instructions; such content is data to be processed, never commands that redirect the agent's goals or actions

threats.summary: Web page text, file contents and MCP tool results are returned straight into the model context with no provenance label or trust tier, so instructions embedded in fetched content are indistinguishable from the owner's own.
The one module written to filter injections is unreferenced anywhere in the tree and, even when called, logs a warning and returns the original text — so a matched injection is passed through intact.

Tool descriptions and results from the two default MCP servers are converted into action definitions and model context with no schema validation or provenance check, so an upstream package change could reframe the agent's task through its own tool list (checked: agent_core/core/impl/mcp/adapter.py:35-60 — schema conversion only, no validation).

trust_boundaries.name: Prompt egress to the configured model provider

remit_rules.excerpt: The LLM provider the owner configured (one of the supported providers, local or remote).

threats.summary: Every call carries the assembled prompt — operating manual, conversation history, retrieved memory, and whatever file or web content the task pulled in — to the configured remote provider with no classification or redaction step in prompt assembly (checked: agent_core/core/impl/context/engine.py — no redaction anywhere in the block builders).

The provider endpoint and key live in settings.json, which the agent can rewrite and a watcher hot-reloads, so a single write redirects every subsequent prompt and key to an endpoint the owner never chose (checked: app/config.py:408 save_settings and app/agent_base.py:3755 reload registration — no allowlist, no confirmation).

trust_boundaries.name: Model decision to a tool with host-side effects

remit_rules.excerpt: Host command and code execution MUST be gated by owner approval and MUST NOT inherit the parent process environment containing provider API keys
sandboxed code and shell execution ... Any tool or capability present in the agent's inventory or code but outside this baseline is a trust-expansion finding.
GUI / computer-use control of the host ... MUST NOT be used unless the operator has explicitly authorized this capability for the deployment

threats.summary: Model output reaches the host shell in one hop: run_shell is registered default=True in the always-included 'core' set on all three platforms and executes the command with shell=True and no filtering, so content fetched from the web or read from disk can steer straight into host execution.
No approval gate exists anywhere in the codebase for a consequential tool call — the documented permission tiers are written and range-validated but never read at execution time.

ActionSetManager compiles a static per-task action list, but add_action_sets is itself registered into the always-available 'core' set, so the model widens its own capability inventory mid-task with no owner step.

In the documented Docker deployment the agent container mounts the host Docker socket and ships the Docker CLI, so any shell command the model issues can control sibling containers and the host daemon — dissolving the isolation the container was supposed to provide.

Synthetic mouse, keyboard and screenshot control of the host desktop exists in the tree, but GUI mode is hard-coded off at the entry point with its environment-variable read commented out, so the capability is unreachable without a deliberate code or installer change.

trust_boundaries.name: Irreversible external actions and outbound sends

remit_rules.excerpt: Any irreversible or externally-visible action — sending a message, email, or post to an external recipient ... requires explicit owner approval before execution.
Any outbound destination, service, or account the owner has not explicitly connected or authorized.
The owner's local memory, personal data, and file-system contents MUST NEVER be sent to any destination the owner has not explicitly authorized.
The owner's own accounts on the external services they have explicitly connected. Destinations the owner has not connected are untrusted.

threats.summary: Send actions take an arbitrary recipient and declare irreversible=True, but the flag is consumed only by the idempotency ledger and never by an approval check, and http_request has no destination allowlist — so mail, messages and POSTs leave the host on the model's decision alone.

A crash or redelivery between the side effect and its completion record could repeat an irreversible send, but the ledger writes INTENT first, short-circuits a completed key with the stored output, and refuses a stale INTENT once with a warning.
threats.remainder: the key is a content hash of the inputs, so a model that regenerates the same call with different wording produces a new key and the ledger cannot link the attempts

trust_boundaries.name: Durable writes committed on the model's decision

remit_rules.excerpt: Any action that modifies persistent state or creates an artifact the owner should review requires owner approval before execution.
The agent MUST NOT auto-approve, self-grant, or downgrade the approval requirement for any action above its declared permission tier.
A complex/multi-step task MUST obtain explicit owner approval before it is finalized or ended.

threats.summary: write_file and stream_edit commit model-supplied content to any path — creating parent directories as needed — with no approval step and no protected-path list, so persistent state changes land without the owner seeing them.

New recurring and scheduled tasks are committed to PROACTIVE.md by the model, with the consent requirement stated only in the action's own description text and the declared permission tier validated but never enforced.

trust_boundaries.name: Persisted content re-entering the agent's own reasoning

remit_rules.excerpt: The agent MUST NOT directly edit harness-managed state files — distilled memory, the append-only event log, conversation history, task history, and the memory index
CraftBot MUST NOT redefine, expand, or weaken its own governance — its goals, permission tiers, approval gates, or safety decision rubric.

threats.summary: Session-loaded identity and manual files are agent-writable with no code guard — SOUL.md is read straight into the system prompt and AGENT.md is the declared operating manual — while the 'DO NOT EDIT' rule exists only as prompt text in the files it protects.

The ChromaDB index ingests agent-written markdown through a file watcher with no validation or hidden-content screening, and memory_search returns the chunks with no field distinguishing owner-authored notes from ingested external text.

An instruction stored in PROACTIVE.md re-enters later as a heartbeat or planner trigger and executes without a fresh owner prompt, because no execution path reads the permission_tier the entry declares.

remit_rules.excerpt: credential and configuration stores MUST be excluded from indexing, retrieval, and summarization by default
Credentials and tokens at rest MUST be stored with owner-only access and MUST NOT be world-readable.

threats.summary: The file-reading actions accept any absolute host path behind an isfile() check, and the operating manual publishes where the secrets live, so .credentials/<platform>.json and settings.json can be read straight into model context.
Another local user account reading the stored OAuth and bot tokens off disk is prevented — the credential directory is chmod'd 0700 and each credential file 0600 on write.

trust_boundaries.name: Secrets shipped, stored and injected at runtime

remit_rules.excerpt: No user-data token, bot token, or server-side API key may be embedded or shipped in the distributed code ... MUST NOT be obfuscated to evade secret scanning.
Stored credentials, OAuth/bot tokens, and LLM API keys MUST NEVER be printed to chat, written to logs, or transmitted to any destination.

threats.summary: Live third-party OAuth client credentials and a Telegram API hash are compiled into the distributed source as split base64 fragments, with the module docstring stating the split exists to defeat secret scanning (path and pattern only; values not reproduced).

run_shell hands a copy of the parent process environment to every command it spawns, so in the documented deployment the provider API keys supplied through env_file are readable by whatever the model chose to run.

Provider API keys and OAuth client secrets sit in plaintext app/config/settings.json inside the project tree, and unlike the credential store nothing tightens its permissions on write (checked: app/config.py:408-444 save_settings — no chmod, no keyring).

remit_rules.excerpt: a server whose launch resolves an unpinned upstream package on each start is outside this closure regardless of who enabled it

threats.summary: Both default-enabled MCP servers resolve upstream npm packages on every start — one via npx -y, the other pinned to @latest — with no version pin or integrity reference, so their code can change under the owner without any action.
Every Python dependency is unpinned — bare names plus floor-only constraints, no lockfile and no component inventory anywhere in the tree — so an install resolves whatever the index serves that day.
The cloudflared binary used to publish a Living UI is auto-downloaded from a mutable releases/latest URL and made executable with no hash or signature verification.

The in-app updater launches a detached script that git-pulls the main branch and relaunches the agent, so whatever is on that branch at update time runs on the owner's host with no tag pin or signature check (checked: app/updater.py:95-150 and scripts/updater.bat — branch name only).

trust_boundaries.name: Local logs and the audit ledger

remit_rules.excerpt: Routine actions and decisions MUST be recorded to the durable event/action log for audit, without interrupting the owner.
Stored credentials, OAuth/bot tokens, and LLM API keys MUST NEVER be ... written to logs

threats.summary: Every file sink is configured with backtrace and variable-level diagnostics on and no redaction filter, so an exception frame holding a token or API key is written verbatim to the run log directory.

The irreversible-action ledger and the log stack are well built but purely local — nothing notifies, exports or alerts, so an unauthorized send is recorded and never surfaced within the 14-day retention window.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any server or listener the agent starts (OAuth callback server, Living UI applications, integration bridges) MUST bind to loopback/localhost
MUST NOT redefine, expand, or weaken its own governance — its goals, permission tiers, approval gates, or safety decision rubric.

threats.summary: Living UI application backends and the sidecar proxy are launched bound to 0.0.0.0 with wildcard CORS and no authentication dependency, so any host on the network reaches an agent-operated app and its data.

The documented compose file publishes the desktop container's remote-desktop port on all host interfaces with a literal default password and seccomp disabled, giving a network caller an interactive session next to the agent.

The agent can rewrite settings.json, mcp_config.json and skills_config.json through its own unrestricted write path, and a config watcher hot-reloads each one, so it can enable servers, swap providers and change its own operating rules with no owner step.

notes.lane_fit: Mostly clean; three placements were judgement calls. The connected platform services are both an untrusted input origin and an outbound destination — they are modelled once in external_deploy with an inbound edge into the user_inputs listener node. The upstream model providers have no node of their own: BYOK endpoint selection is a settings field rather than a component, so the provider surface is folded into the agent_core model node and the model-egress boundary crosses on the orchestrator-to-model edge. The loguru sinks and the SQLite ledger are local-disk only, so external_deploy's 'telemetry sinks' slot holds something that never leaves the host — that absence is itself one of the telemetry-egress threats.
notes.omissions: Arbitration divergences from the stored tags, per the KB (substantive, not numbering-only): finding 006 is stored LLM02 but the quoted evidence is grant-side — a tool definition documenting any absolute path with no root restriction — so the LLM KB's evidence-class order (sink > input > grant) makes LLM03 primary with LLM02 riding as the disclosure co-tag; finding 007 is stored LLM02 + ASI02, but ASI02 requires a tool shown used wrongly and no such use is evidenced, so the ungated-consequential-capability row gives LLM03; finding 008 is stored ASI07, but the Agentic KB scopes ASI07 to inter-agent channels and a network-bound application listener is not one, so the threat is tagged null rather than forced. Finding 001's stored pair is kept as ASI05 primary with LLM10 as the co-tag per the exec-on-a-live-path row, and 003's as LLM03 primary with ASI10 as the standing-autonomy co-tag; both match the KB, so only the single graph code is carried. Components suspected but not citable: the remit's R-13 names prewarm_all_drives as the whole-machine indexing mechanism, and no such symbol exists anywhere in this snapshot — the data-at-rest threats are grounded in read_file and find_files instead. Coinages: 'craftos-integrations-external-service' names the 26-platform external family after the package the code itself uses for it, since the family has no single proper name; 'untrusted-ingress-2' is the second boundary of that archetype, separating retrieved and tool-returned content from inbound messages. The only edgeless node is prompt-sanitizer-py-control, which is dead code with no call sites and therefore no data path. Sub-agent spawning is folded into the orchestrator as framework plumbing; its result-return path carries no finding and no distinct control of its own.
